lessons.title: Trending Markets and the Death of Reversion Signals

children.text: Lesson 1's structural break was about one company: a specific, identifiable event permanently changing one stock's parameters. This lesson is about a different, broader failure mode. Sometimes reversion signals across an entire watchlist, in completely unrelated sectors, with no shared company-specific news at all, start failing at the same time. That is not six separate structural breaks happening to coincide. It is the market itself, the regime this course opened with in Chapter 1, Lesson 2, having quietly shifted from range-bound to trending, and every reversion strategy built on the range-bound assumption paying the price together.

body.text: A single stock's structural break and a market-wide regime shift into a trend look identical from inside one failing trade, but they are diagnosed differently. One stock failing while everything else in the watchlist behaves normally points to that stock specifically. Many unrelated stocks failing at once points to the regime itself, and no amount of per-stock fundamental research fixes a problem that lives at the market level.

children.text: Reading the Regime Off the Index Itself

Chapter 3, Lesson 3's moving-average slope filter was built for a single stock, but the exact same tool applies directly to the Nifty 50 itself. A market where the index has been oscillating around a fairly flat 50 or 200-day moving average for months is the range-bound environment mean reversion strategies are built for. A market where the index's own moving average has a strong, sustained slope, in either direction, for an extended stretch is a trending environment, and individual stock reversion signals inside it are swimming against a genuine tide, not exploiting a temporary overreaction.

body.title: Nifty 50: range-bound stretch vs trending stretch (illustrative)

body.text: Months 1 through 6 are a textbook range-bound regime: the index crosses its own moving average repeatedly, exactly the environment single-asset reversion strategies are designed for. From month 7, the moving average itself starts climbing steadily, the same slope signature Chapter 3 flagged for a single stock, now visible in the index. Every stock's reversion signal built during months 1 to 6 is now operating inside a fundamentally different market.

children.text: Market Breadth: A Second Confirming Signal

markDefs.definition: The percentage of stocks in a broad index participating in the prevailing trend, commonly measured as the share of stocks trading above their own 200-day moving average.

children.text: The Nifty's own slope is one signal.

, the percentage of NSE-listed stocks trading above their own 200-day moving average, available on most Indian stock screeners, is a second, independent confirmation. A very high or very low breadth reading, most stocks trending the same direction at once, describes a market where individual stock idiosyncrasies are being overwhelmed by a common, market-wide force, precisely when single-asset reversion signals are least trustworthy.

Reduce position sizing and trading frequency across the book, rather than forcing trades

body.text: The recommended response is to reduce exposure, not to abandon mean reversion permanently or to switch untested into a momentum strategy overnight. Regimes shift back. A trending market eventually resumes chopping, and a strategy that stepped back rather than fighting the tide is in a far better position to re-engage than one that kept forcing trades and depleting its risk budget throughout the trend.

body.title: Compute the target-exit rate during a trend
body.prompt: Across a watchlist's trailing 20 reversion signals during a confirmed trending period, 4 hit their target, 12 hit their stop-loss, and 4 timed out. What percentage of signals reached their target?
body.explanation: 4 out of 20 is 20%, well below the 55 to 60% typical of a range-bound regime, and a clear portfolio-level warning that the strategy is operating inside a trending market.

body.title: Regime shift or single-stock structural break?
body.question: Six stocks across banking, IT, and FMCG sectors, with no shared news event connecting them, have each failed their last three to four reversion signals in a row. Is this better explained by a market-wide regime shift or a company-specific structural break?
options: A company-specific structural break, since each stock should be researched individually for bad news
A market-wide regime shift, since unrelated stocks across different sectors failing simultaneously points to something affecting the whole market, not one company
Neither, this pattern has no diagnostic meaning at all
It is impossible to distinguish these two situations under any circumstances
body.explanation: Lesson 1's structural break is diagnosed when one stock fails while the rest of the watchlist behaves normally. Multiple, sector-unrelated stocks failing at the same time, with no shared company-specific catalyst, points instead to the regime itself, exactly the case this lesson covers, best checked against the Nifty's own moving-average slope and market breadth, not against any single company's fundamentals.

cards.definition: A market-wide change from a range-bound, mean-reverting environment to a trending one, or vice versa, affecting many unrelated stocks simultaneously rather than one company specifically.
The percentage of stocks in a broad index participating in the prevailing trend, commonly measured as the share trading above their own 200-day moving average.
The percentage of a strategy's signals that resolve via the target exit rather than a stop-loss or timeout, a portfolio-level health check that degrades sharply during a hostile, trending regime.

points: A market-wide regime shift into a trend and a single-stock structural break can look identical from inside one failing trade, but they are diagnosed differently: one stock failing alone points to that stock, many unrelated stocks failing together points to the regime.
The Nifty's own moving-average slope, using exactly Chapter 3's single-stock slope filter applied to the index, is a direct, practical read on whether the broader market is range-bound or trending.
Market breadth, the percentage of stocks trading above their own 200-day moving average, is a second, independent confirmation of the same regime read.

A trending regime shows up as a portfolio-level statistic: the target-exit rate across a whole watchlist falling sharply while stop-loss rates rise, a broader version of Lesson 1's single-stock failed-reversion signal.

The correct response to a confirmed trending regime is reduced position sizing and trading frequency, not abandoning mean reversion permanently, since regimes shift back and a strategy that stepped back can re-engage when they do.
